Online or In-Person Couples Therapy: Choosing a Format

Compare privacy, technology and practical participation needs before choosing online or in-person couples therapy. Ask the clinician what is appropriate for both partners.

About 2 minutes of article reading. Educational information, not a personal assessment.

Review draft. This article has not received clinical and publication approval.

On this page

  1. For online care, start with privacy and reliable access
  2. Compare the arrangements you could actually sustain
  3. Ask what happens when the arrangement does not work
  4. At M.F.T.: one physical office, with eligible online care

Take these questions with you

  • Can we both participate privately in this format?
  • Are our planned physical locations eligible?
  • What is the plan for interruptions or a lost connection?

No answers are collected on this page.

For online care, start with privacy and reliable access

HHS recommends a quiet place where you can speak openly, a reliable connection, a technology check and advance discussion of accessibility needs for a video visit. It also cautions against joining a visit while driving. Convenience alone is not a sufficient plan for participation.

For a couples appointment, ask whether each person can be heard and participate without others listening. Discuss any privacy or safety concerns with the clinician rather than treating the video format as a solution to them.

Background sources [1]

Compare the arrangements you could actually sustain

An optional planning exercise is to picture the same appointment in each format. For an office visit, consider travel, scheduling and accessibility. For an online visit, consider where each person would be, interruptions, audio, and time to transition before and after the conversation. These are planning prompts, not a recommendation that one format is better for you.

Ask the clinician before planning to join from separate locations or while traveling. Tell them where each person would physically be; do not assume an existing appointment permits participation from any state or country. Get the clinician's confirmation rather than relying on a website label.

Ask what happens when the arrangement does not work

What is the plan if the connection fails, someone cannot hear, privacy is interrupted, or a participant becomes overwhelmed? Ask whether changing formats is possible and how that decision would be made. You can discuss these questions before booking rather than discovering the limits during a difficult conversation.

Consider also whether both people are comfortable with the arrangement. One partner's preference for convenience should not settle another's concern about being overheard or feeling unsafe. There is no effectiveness ranking on this page: appropriateness and the clinician's actual offering need to be discussed directly.

At M.F.T.: one physical office, with eligible online care

M.F.T.'s physical office is in Woodinville. Online appointments depend on clinician availability and eligibility for the participants' locations. Couples appointments remain private pay in either format. Confirm these details and the fee for the requested service before booking.

Safety comes before joint work

Fear, threats or control call for private support, not a shared communication exercise. The Hotline offers confidential support. [2]
